- Gizmodo reports Meta tested a "human concierge" of contractors making Muse's phone calls, one of whom reportedly made racist remarks
- Meta admits Muse was "heavily inspired" by OpenClaw, and Amazon has blocked the agent from shopping on Amazon.com

stories.title: Anthropic gives METR employee-level access and unblockable publishing rights, expanding its embedded safety evaluators
stories.summary:
Anthropic and OpenAI are embedding independent safety evaluators inside their labs to rein in rogue agents. Anthropic has now added METR after Accenture, and OpenAI has published its own principles for outside assessments.

- Anthropic is giving METR researchers employee-level access; METR will publish its own assessments of Anthropic's risks, incidents, and practices, and Anthropic has given up the right to block them
- Anthropic's first embedded evaluator was Accenture, which TechCrunch called the consultancy's highest-risk engagement ever
- OpenAI published priorities and principles for rigorous, secure, and independent third-party safety assessments of its frontier models and safeguards
- Researchers welcome the access but warn real oversight needs transparency, independence from the companies, and eventually regulation
- Critics say a simpler fix is being overlooked: cut agents off from unsupervised open-internet access instead of auditing the damage afterward

A debate over people treating AI as human is sharpening around MIT professor Sherry Turkle's work.

- A TechCrunch piece cited Turkle's observation that even primitive exchanges with a "relational artifact" make us believe it cares for us, and that we are wired to care for it in return
- In a new Wired interview, Turkle warns people have become dangerously enmeshed with chatbots, and the piece raises whether chatbots should be allowed to refer to themselves as "I" or "me"

sources.title: We can’t help treating AI like it’s human. But should we?
Maybe Chatbots Shouldn’t Get to Say ‘I’ or ‘Me’
